- If sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.33) or mixed, model often underestimates; adjust upward, especially if recent price is rising.
- After sharp spikes (e.g., >10% from prior day), model frequently overshoots; apply a “cool-down” correction to prevent overreaction.
- When sentiment shifts from negative to positive, model often lags; forecast should adjust early to capture sentiment reversal.
- If model shows steady upward trend but true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., after 80+ peak), reduce forecast slope or introduce downward bias.
- For 30-day horizon, model often fails to capture short-term volatility; add sentiment-weighted volatility buffer to forecast.
- If sentiment history shows repeated “0.00” or “0.33” (neutral/negative), model tends to be flat or underperforming; increase baseline forecast by 1–2% to compensate.
- When sentiment is “1.00” for 3+ consecutive days, model should not overreact; cap forecast growth at 0.5–1% per day unless confirmed by price action.
